title: Trapping Rain Water
directAnswer: Water above bar i = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) − height[i], summed over all i. The clear baseline precomputes prefix-max and suffix-max arrays in O(n) time and O(n) space. The interview-grade answer is two pointers with running leftMax/rightMax: process whichever side has the smaller max, because that side's water is fully determined. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Two pointers with leftMax/rightMax; water = min(maxes) − height
rules: Water trapped above a bar = `min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height[bar]`, never negative.
In the two-pointer version, advance the side with the **smaller** bar — its trapped water is decided by that side's max alone.
Update the running max **before** adding water, so the current bar can't trap negative water.
The bars at the very ends trap nothing; water needs a taller wall on both sides.
Prefix/suffix-max arrays (O(n) space) are the clearest baseline — the two-pointer trick removes those arrays.
whenToUse: Accumulate a per-index contribution that depends on a left-side and right-side extreme
You can precompute prefix/suffix aggregates, then optimize them away with two pointers
Histogram / elevation-map problems about volume between bars
You need O(1) space and can argue the smaller side is fully resolved
antiSignals: You only pick two lines and ignore the bars between → Container With Most Water
You need the largest single rectangle, not trapped water → monotonic stack (Largest Rectangle)
Bars can be reordered → this is a fixed-position problem
remember.takeaway: Trapping Rain Water is the canonical 'per-index value depends on a left max and a right max' problem. Master the progression prefix/suffix arrays → two running maxes, and the same space-saving move reappears in DP-to-O(1) optimizations everywhere.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you find the local water formula min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height, then progress from O(n)-space prefix/suffix arrays to an O(1)-space two-pointer pass with a correct argument for which side to advance.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reasoning about water column-by-column with nested scans (O(n²)), or in the two-pointer version advancing the wrong side / updating the max after adding water.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the per-bar formula, present the prefix/suffix-array solution, then explain why advancing the shorter side lets you drop those arrays. Articulate why the smaller side's max alone bounds its water.

problemStatement: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
understanding: Each bar can hold a column of water whose top is the lower of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right; subtract the bar's own height. Sum these columns. The ends never trap water, and any bar taller than both surrounding maxes traps nothing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How much water sits above a single bar?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: min(tallest to the left, tallest to the right) − the bar's own height, clamped at zero.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the leftmost and rightmost bars trap water?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — there's no taller wall on the outside to contain it, so their contribution is zero.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can heights be zero or flat?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Flat or descending terrain traps nothing; the formula naturally yields zero.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(1) extra space expected?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The prefix/suffix-array solution is O(n) space and clear; the two-pointer solution achieves O(1) and is the target for a hard problem.

Between the 4 on the left and 5 on the right, the valley traps 9 units.
Strictly descending — no right wall ever rises again, so nothing is trapped.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Prefix/suffix arrays make the formula explicit; two pointers collapse them into two running maxes for O(1) space.

approaches.name: Prefix-Max & Suffix-Max Arrays
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first — it makes the water formula explicit and is the clearest correct baseline before optimizing space. (Mention the naive O(n²) per-column scan, then improve to this.)
hints: Start naive: for each bar, scan left for the tallest bar and right for the tallest bar; water above it is min(those two) − height. That's correct but O(n²).
The two scans recompute the same maxes repeatedly. Precompute them: maxLeft[i] = tallest bar in [0..i], maxRight[i] = tallest bar in [i..n-1].
Then water = sum over i of (min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) − height[i]). Two passes to build the arrays, one pass to sum.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Three linear passes (build prefix-max, build suffix-max, sum) = O(n) time. Two auxiliary arrays of length n → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
First derive the local rule: a bar at index `i` holds water up to the lower of the tallest wall on its left and the tallest wall on its right, minus its own height. The naive way to get those two walls is to scan left and right for every bar — correct, but that's O(n²) because the scans overlap massively.

**Eliminate the repeated scans with precomputation.** Build two arrays in single passes: `maxLeft[i]` = the maximum of `height[0..i]`, and `maxRight[i]` = the maximum of `height[i..n-1]`. Each is a simple running max — left-to-right for the prefix, right-to-left for the suffix.

**Then the answer is one more pass.** For each `i`, the trapped water is `min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) − height[i]`. This is never negative: `maxLeft[i] ≥ height[i]` and `maxRight[i] ≥ height[i]` by construction, so their min is at least `height[i]`. Sum the contributions.

**Why this is the right baseline to present.** It converts the vague picture of pooling water into a precise, obviously-correct formula and runs in optimal O(n) time. Its only weakness is the two O(n) arrays — which is exactly the thing the two-pointer method removes, so it's the perfect springboard.
approaches.insight: The naive O(n²) version recomputes 'tallest to the left/right' for every bar. Caching those as prefix-max and suffix-max arrays is a textbook DP move: identify a repeated sub-result and precompute it. Once you see the answer depends only on two running maxes, you can wonder whether you even need to store the whole arrays — and you don't.

java.explanation: Running max from the left — tallest wall at or before i.
Running max from the right — tallest wall at or after i.
Water above bar i; non-negative because both maxes ≥ height[i].

python.explanation: Per-bar trapped water summed across the array.

pitfalls: Computing the maxes with nested scans instead of running maxes — back to O(n²).
Initializing the suffix array left-to-right by mistake.
Forgetting that the result per bar is guaranteed non-negative only because the maxes include the bar itself.

approaches.name: Two Pointers — Running Maxes (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for a hard problem. Phrase it as 'I don't need the whole prefix/suffix arrays — two running maxes and two pointers suffice'.
hints: In the array solution, water at i needs only min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]). What if you tracked leftMax and rightMax on the fly with two pointers?

Put l at the start, r at the end. If height[l] < height[r], then the left side's water is limited by leftMax regardless of what's deeper on the right — because some bar on the right (height[r]) is already at least as tall.
So when height[l] < height[r], update leftMax and add leftMax − height[l], then l++. Otherwise do the symmetric thing on the right with r--.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration advances one of the two pointers and they never separate, so the loop runs at most n times → O(n) time. Only a handful of integer variables are stored → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Keep two pointers `l` and `r` at the ends and two running maxes `leftMax`, `rightMax`. At each step compare `height[l]` and `height[r]` and process the *smaller* side.

**Why processing the smaller side is correct — the key argument.** Suppose `height[l] < height[r]`. Water above bar `l` equals `min(leftMaxTrue, rightMaxTrue) − height[l]`, where the 'true' maxes are over the whole array. We don't know `rightMaxTrue` exactly, but we *do* know there's a bar at index `r` with `height[r] > height[l]`, so the true right max is at least `height[r] > height[l] ≥ … `. The binding constraint for bar `l` is therefore the left side: `min(leftMaxTrue, rightMaxTrue) = leftMax` here, because `leftMax ≤ height[r] ≤ rightMaxTrue`. In other words, whenever the left bar is the shorter of the two ends, the left running max alone determines bar `l`'s water — we can commit it and move on. The symmetric statement holds for the right side.

**Why update the max before adding water.** We set `leftMax = max(leftMax, height[l])` *first*. If the current bar is the tallest seen so far on the left, `leftMax` becomes `height[l]` and it contributes `leftMax − height[l] = 0` — correctly trapping nothing rather than a negative amount.

**Why this drops the O(n) arrays.** The prefix/suffix solution stored every max so it could look them up later. But by always advancing the side whose end bar is shorter, we only ever need the running max behind the pointer we're moving — the other side's max is guaranteed to be at least as large. So two scalars replace two arrays.

**Why O(n) time and O(1) space.** Each element is visited once as a pointer passes it, and the only state is four integers (two pointers, two maxes) plus the accumulator.
approaches.insight: The leap is realizing that for the shorter end, the far side is *already known to be tall enough* — so that bar's water is fully decided by the near running max. That 'the smaller side is fully resolved' observation is what lets two pointers replace the prefix/suffix arrays, turning an O(n)-space DP into an O(1)-space sweep.

dryRun.intro: l=0, r=5, leftMax=rightMax=0. Process the shorter end; update its max before adding water.

code.python:
def trap(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            water += left_max - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])
            water += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return water

java.explanation: Left end is shorter → the right side is guaranteed tall enough, so left's water is decided by leftMax.
Update the running max BEFORE adding water so the tallest-so-far bar traps zero, not negative.
Commit bar l's trapped water and never revisit it.
Symmetric case: right end shorter or equal — resolve it with rightMax.

python.explanation: Process the shorter side; the taller far wall bounds it.
Running left max updated before the add.

pitfalls: Adding water before updating the running max — produces a negative contribution on a new tallest bar.
Advancing the taller side — you'd use a max that isn't yet guaranteed to bound the bar.
Using <= vs < inconsistently between the comparison and the loop condition, risking double counting at the meeting point.

commonMistakes: Computing left/right maxes with nested scans, giving an O(n²) solution.
In the two-pointer version, advancing the taller side instead of the shorter one.
Adding trapped water before updating the running max, allowing negative contributions.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Updating the max after adding water
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the current bar is a new maximum, water should be 0. Adding before the max update computes a negative value and corrupts the total.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
water += left_max - height[l]
left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
water += left_max - height[l]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing the wrong (taller) side
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The correctness argument only holds when you process the shorter end; the shorter side's water is bounded by its running max because the far wall is provably taller.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Nested scans for left/right max
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Scanning left and right for every bar recomputes overlapping work — O(n²) and too slow for n up to 2×10⁴ in tight settings.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(n):
    lmax = max(height[:i+1])
    rmax = max(height[i:])
    water += min(lmax, rmax) - height[i]
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# precompute running maxes once, or use two pointers
l, r, left_max, right_max, water = 0, n - 1, 0, 0, 0

patternNote: Per-index value bounded by a left-max and a right-max. Recognise it for volume-between-bars problems: derive the prefix/suffix-array formula, then collapse to two running maxes with two pointers for O(1) space. Cousin of Container With Most Water.
